attempts.answer:
Below is a practical toolkit of validated questionnaires, scales, and design tools to assess and steward an "Intentional University"—an ecosystem that balances purposeful, goal-directed learning with intentional design for serendipity and discovery. The instruments are grouped by construct (intentionality, learning processes, serendipity/discovery, social/relational climate, and enabling environments), with guidance on use and caveats.

1) What "Intentional University" asks us to measure
- Intentionality and self-regulated learning: goal-directed learning behaviors, learning intentions, self-efficacy, and personal resolve.
- Serendipity and discovery: frequency and quality of unexpected, valuable insights; novelty/unexpectedness and usefulness of encounters.
- Social/relational climate: relating to others, community and mentoring affordances that catalyze discovery.
- Equity and belonging: perceived fairness in opportunities, processes, and outcomes as prerequisites for engaged intentionality.
- Enabling environments: physical and digital spaces that restore attention, support exploration, and enable chance encounters.

2) Psychometric instruments adapted for higher-education contexts

Intentionality, motivation, and self-regulation
- Personal resolve and self-efficacy (adapted Likert scales). Example items operationalize "I will do whatever it takes to master my academic studies" and "I expect to do well academically," with reliability estimates around .70–.85 in university samples; these capture students' intentions and self-efficacy for academic learning and can be used to benchmark goal-directed engagement on your campus. <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">We used existing Likert-scale inventories to measure concepts; Personal Resolve and Personal Self-Efficacy were adapted from established sources with reliability estimates .85 and .72 respectively, showing feasibility for higher-education measurement</cite>.
- Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) subscales (adapted). The MSLQ's self-efficacy and self-regulation subscales are frequently adapted for university surveys; they provide validated item pools to assess goal-setting, effort regulation, and volitional control central to intentional learning. <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">Personal Self-Efficacy was adapted from the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (Pintrich et al., 1993)</cite>.

Serendipity and serendipitous learning
- Operationalized serendipity items (novelty, unexpectedness, usefulness). Studies report using paired post-task Likerts and open-ended probes to capture perceived interestingness, novelty, and unexpectedness of recommendations or encounters; combining quantitative ratings with qualitative feedback helps parse the components of serendipity experienced in learning systems and spaces. <cite id="b3bef86f-0">Serendipity was measured with two post-task 0–5 ratings of interestingness; authors note this high-level indicator may miss novelty and unexpectedness, recommending item-level ratings and qualitative feedback to capture serendipity nuances</cite> <cite id="b3bef86f-1">Serendipity-enhancing systems can be designed by supporting internal, external factors, and exploratory behavior, providing a framework to operationalize serendipity in learning environments</cite>.
- Conceptual definitions to inform item development. Literature distinguishes serendipity as unexpected realizations of hidden connections, exploration guided by skills and goals, and by-product discoveries during planned tasks; these definitions support constructing items that target "unexpected yet valuable insights," "connecting unconnected ideas," and "productive tangents." <cite id="b3bef86f-2">Serendipitous learning emphasizes unexpected realization of hidden connections; surprising information and unexpected social relationships can lead to meaningful learning and enhance exploratory behavior</cite>.
- Minimal serendipity probes for pilots. Short Likert items plus one open question can quickly assess perceived usefulness of random exploration and serendipity in a campus or classroom context. <cite id="b3bef86f-3">Questionnaires can include 5-point Likert items on random exploration and serendipity plus an open question about usefulness, providing a lightweight operationalization</cite>.

Social/relational climate and belonging
- Relating to others (LOSO-based). Adapted LOSO items (e.g., "I find it easy to relate to others at university") provide a reliable measure of students' relational functioning and social connectedness; these can be used to assess mentoring, peer learning networks, and community climate that enable collaborative discovery. <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">Relating to Others was adapted from the LOSO Questionnaire (Van Damme et al., 2002) with reliability estimate .72</cite>.
- Social milieu and inclusion. Adapted items gauge whether the university milieu is welcoming and accepting of diversity—conditions that support intentional learning and openness to novel perspectives. <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">The Social Milieu subscale (adapted items) measured perceived welcoming and accepting climate with reliability estimate .83</cite>.
- Sense of educational equity. A validated 19-item questionnaire across three dimensions—equity in opportunities, process, and outcomes—offers a compact, well-tested instrument to assess whether students perceive fair access and treatment, which is foundational for intentional engagement and risk-taking in discovery. <cite id="f4706e52-1">A 19-item questionnaire on sense of equity (opportunities, process, outcomes) using a 5-point Likert scale showed Cronbach's alpha >.7 for each dimension</cite>.

Enabling environments: physical/digital spaces and restoration
- Rest@U: perceived restorativeness of the university environment. Validated in Italian universities, Rest@U captures restorative qualities of campus spaces that restore attention and reduce cognitive fatigue—key enablers of deep, intentional study—and notes cross-context validation and longitudinal designs as future improvements. <cite id="05fa2f3a-4">Students' perceived restorativeness of the university environment (Rest@U) was validated, with cautions about generalizability and recommendations to collect data across countries and longitudinally</cite>.
- Staff QoL and organizational supports (TASQ@work). Although focused on staff, TASQ@work demonstrates university-context psychometrics for organizational meaning, support, and identification; such dimensions can be adapted to student-facing services (e.g., advising, libraries) that mediate intentional learning experiences. <cite id="05fa2f3a-0">TASQ@work showed good psychometric properties in academia with noted limitations (e.g., RMSEA, limited generalizability) and recommendations for larger, more differentiated samples</cite>.

3) Tools and design instruments to operationalize intentionality and serendipity

Design probes and recommendation engines for serendipity
- Serendipity-inducing recommender systems. Interactive evolutionary computation recommenders can surface "productive tangents," with evaluation via item-level novelty/unexpectedness and usefulness ratings plus interviews; this provides a two-way toolkit—both measure and design intervention—for campus learning platforms and resource discovery. <cite id="b3bef86f-0">To induce serendipity, systems can prompt item-level ratings of novelty and unexpectedness beyond overall interestingness, triangulated with qualitative interviews</cite> <cite id="b3bef86f-1">Designing for internal, external factors and exploratory behavior yields a structured approach to facilitate serendipity while maintaining learner agency</cite>.
- Open online networks and personal learning environments. Work in personal learning environments shows how content aggregation and social links increase the probability of serendipitous connections; you can adapt campus LMS or social tools to foster cross-disciplinary pathways and evaluate with serendipity probes. <cite id="b3bef86f-2">Serendipity is more probable in open online learning contexts where learners traverse varied resources and activities; it supports connection building, discovery, and creativity</cite>.

Proximity and chance-encounter tools
- Proximity-based recommendation criteria. Campus tools that layer profile similarity, physical/geographic proximity, and randomized exploration can be evaluated with short Likert scales and open-ended usefulness prompts; these mechanics operationalize serendipity and can be embedded in campus apps. <cite id="b3bef86f-3">Survey steps combining 5-point Likerts on random exploration and serendipity with an open question on usefulness provide a template for evaluating serendipity interventions</cite>.
- Knowledge-sharing infrastructures. Knowledge-sharing ecosystems that surface surprising connections can be studied via knowledge mapping and social network analyses; qualitative accounts emphasize the role of chance encounters and social proximity as catalysts, suggesting dashboards that track serendipity events and their outcomes. <cite id="b3bef86f-2">Surprising information and unexpected social relationships can lead to meaningful learning and enhance exploratory behavior in learning networks</cite>.

4) Putting it together: a measurement blueprint for the Intentional University

Core survey battery (baseline)
- Intentionality and volition: Personal Resolve and Self-Efficacy (adapted 5-point Likert items), plus an optional MSLQ self-regulation subscale. <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">Adapted Personal Resolve and Personal Self-Efficacy subscales with reliability around .85 and .72 demonstrate feasible measurement in higher-education samples</cite>.
- Social and belonging climate: Relating to Others (LOSO-based); Social Milieu (welcoming/accepting); Sense of Educational Equity (three dimensions). <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">Relating to Others and Social Milieu subscales adapted from LOSO and established instruments</cite> <cite id="f4706e52-1">Equity questionnaire with three dimensions and Cronbach's alpha >.7</cite>.
- Enabling environments: Rest@U perceived restorativeness of campus spaces; add a short module on organizational supports (e.g., advising/IT/mentoring access) adapted from TASQ@work constructs. <cite id="05fa2f3a-4">Rest@U validation and cautions on generalizability</cite> <cite id="05fa2f3a-0">TASQ@work psychometrics in academia, with recommendations for larger and more differentiated samples</cite>.
- Serendipity and discovery: Baseline serendipity items (overall interestingness, novelty, unexpectedness, usefulness) and an open-ended prompt "Describe a recent serendipitous insight and how it changed your learning." <cite id="b3bef86f-0">Two 0–5 ratings of interestingness and explicit call for item-level novelty/unexpectedness plus qualitative feedback</cite> <cite id="b3bef86f-3">Likert items on random exploration and serendipity plus an open question on usefulness</cite>.
- Demographics and study design notes: cohort, program, prior knowledge/interests, and timing; consider longitudinal waves to assess growth and persistence of serendipity-enabled gains. <cite id="05fa2f3a-4">Longitudinal designs are recommended to evaluate criterion-related validity and reduce common method bias in university context studies</cite>.

Optional experimental add-ons
- Platform/module A/B: Embed a serendipity recommender or randomized "lateral reading" prompt in LMS activities and compare cohorts. Evaluate with item-level novelty/usefulness and interviews/focus groups to understand mechanisms. <cite id="b3bef86f-0">Combining quantitative serendipity ratings with qualitative feedback helps explain how recommendations change learning experiences</cite> <cite id="b3bef86f-1">Serendipity systems should support internal, external factors and exploratory behavior to maintain learner agency</cite>.
- Space-based interventions: Pilot "mix-and-match" zones that juxtapose disciplines; measure perceived restorativeness and social connectedness before/after and correlate with discovery outcomes. <cite id="05fa2f3a-4">Perceived restorativeness is a validated construct sensitive to campus space attributes and suitable for pre-post evaluation</cite>.

5) Reporting and interpretation: what to look for
- Intentionality baseline: High resolve and self-efficacy coupled with strong relating-to-others and equity climate predict more active discovery behaviors; conversely, low restorativeness and weak social milieu signal friction points for intentional learning. <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">Relating to Others and Social Milieu subscales reliably capture relational climate</cite> <cite id="05fa2f3a-4">Rest@U identifies space-related restorative qualities linked to learning capacity</cite>.
- Serendipity signal: Look for positive novelty×usefulness interactions—students report unexpected insights that they applied. Triangulate with qualitative narratives to separate "noise" from "productive serendipity." <cite id="b3bef86f-0">Serendipity requires parsing novelty, unexpectedness, and usefulness; qualitative feedback complements ratings</cite>.
- Equity and belonging as mediators: Mediation analyses often show equity and community climate boosting intentionality and discovery; monitor these pathways to diagnose inequities that mute students' agency. <cite id="f4706e52-1">Sense of equity questionnaire provides a validated lens on perceived fairness across opportunities, process, and outcomes</cite>.
- Psychometric caveats and remedies: Expect context-specificity and common-method variance; collect multi-campus samples, validate factor structures, and mix methods to reduce bias. <cite id="05fa2f3a-0">Academic-scale psychometrics often face RMSEA issues with small samples and limited generalizability; larger, differentiated samples and additional validity tests are recommended</cite> <cite id="05fa2f3a-4">Self-report criterion validity benefits from longitudinal designs and cross-context validation to address generalizability and common method variance</cite>.

6) Quick-start instrument list (validated or adaptable) and where to source them
- Intentionality and self-regulation: Adapted Personal Resolve and Self-Efficacy subscales from Phan et al. and MSLQ item banks; item examples and reliability reported. <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">Adapted Personal Resolve and Self-Efficacy items and reliability estimates are documented</cite>.
- Relational climate: LOSO Questionnaire—Relating to Others subscale. <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">LOSO-based Relating to Others subscale with reliability estimate .72</cite>.
- Equity climate: Sense of Educational Equity questionnaire (19 items; three dimensions). <cite id="f4706e52-1">19-item equity questionnaire with Cronbach's alpha >.7 across dimensions</cite>.
- Enabling environment: Rest@U (perceived restorativeness) and TASQ@work (organizational supports) as prototypes/adaptations. <cite id="05fa2f3a-4">Rest@U scale validated in Italian universities with generalizability caveats</cite> <cite id="05fa2f3a-0">TASQ@work shows good psychometrics in academia with recommendations for improving invariance and generalizability</cite>.
- Serendipity: Baseline Likert probes for interestingness, novelty, unexpectedness, usefulness; add open-ended prompts and interviews; draw on ITC translation/adaptation guidance for multilingual campuses. <cite id="b3bef86f-0">Serendipity measurement via item-level ratings and qualitative feedback</cite> <cite id="b3bef86f-3">Short Likert items plus open-ended usefulness prompts for serendipity</cite> <cite id="05fa2f3a-2">International Test Commission guidance on translation/adaptation supports cross-context deployment</cite>.

7) Actionable next steps for your university
- Build a baseline dashboard: Run a cross-sectional survey combining the above instruments in one tool; segment by school/program; compare with Rest@U and equity climate. <cite id="05fa2f3a-4">Rest@U and equity-based instruments are validated in university contexts and suitable for cross-sectional deployment with caveats</cite>.
- Pilot serendipity features: Launch a discovery module that surfaces cross-disciplinary resources and evaluate with item-level serendipity metrics and interviews; iterate based on novelty×usefulness signals. <cite id="b3bef86f-0">Item-level serendipity ratings and qualitative feedback help isolate what drives value</cite>.
- Co-design spaces and networks: Use Rest@U hot-spots to prioritize restorative redesigns and LOSO-based relating scores to target mentoring/peer-learning hubs; pair with proximity-based recommendation mechanics. <cite id="05fa2f3a-4">Rest@U identifies actionable space attributes for restorativeness</cite> <cite id="b3bef86f-3">Proximity and random exploration items plus usefulness prompts operationalize serendipity in campus tools</cite>.
- Monitor equity and agency: Track changes in equity climate and community connectedness as mediators of increased discovery outcomes; use these insights to close access gaps in serendipity-rich opportunities. <cite id="f4706e52-1">Equity questionnaire provides validated dimensions to monitor and target interventions</cite> <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">Relating to Others and Social Milieu capture connectedness and inclusion</cite>.

Limitations and research needs
- Conceptual clarity: Serendipity is multifaceted; relying on single-item Likerts risks collapsing meaning—use multi-item composites and qualitative methods together. <cite id="b3bef86f-0">Two-item serendipity measures may miss novelty and unexpectedness; item-level probes and interviews are recommended</cite>.
- Generalizability: University-specific validations (e.g., Rest@U in Italy; TASQ@work in two universities) require expansion across institutions and cultures for robust inference. <cite id="05fa2f3a-4">Italian Rest@U study emphasizes generalizability limits and calls for multi-country validation</cite> <cite id="05fa2f3a-0">TASQ@work notes sample size and invariance limitations, recommending larger, differentiated samples</cite>.
- Causal inference: Self-report designs face common-method bias; longitudinal cohorts and mixed methods improve validity. <cite id="05fa2f3a-4">Longitudinal designs and cross-context validation reduce common method variance and improve criterion validity</cite>.

In sum, you can operationalize "Intentional University" with a layered toolkit: intentionality and self-regulation (resolve, efficacy), social/relational and equity climates (belonging, access), enabling environments (restoration, support), and serendipity/discovery (novelty, unexpectedness, usefulness). Use validated instruments where available (Rest@U; LOSO-based; equity; MSLQ/resolve-efficacy) and adapt them to your context, then add targeted serendipity probes and design tools to catalyze discovery pathways. Triangulate quantitative dashboards with qualitative narratives and iterate—this yields an actionable, evidence-based approach to measuring and improving intentionality, serendipity, and discovery in your university. <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">Adapted Likert-scale instruments capture intentionality, relatedness, and efficacy in university settings with acceptable reliability</cite> <cite id="05fa2f3a-4">Perceived restorativeness and organizational supports have validated measures in university contexts, with guidance to expand generalizability</cite> <cite id="b3bef86f-0">Serendipity can be measured through item-level novelty/unexpectedness and usefulness combined with qualitative feedback</cite> <cite id="b3bef86f-2">Serendipity is more likely in open, connected learning environments that support exploration and discovery</cite> <cite id="f4706e52-1">Sense of educational equity questionnaires provide reliable, validated constructs to benchmark and track</cite>.

Snippet: Following the guidelines provided by the International Test Commission (2018), the scales were translated and adapted to ensure their applicability in Chinese higher education. Discrepancies were recorded, and a third team member facilitated the resolution process. The final version of the questionnaire was digitized and uploaded to the 'Wenjuanxing' online survey platform. 

A purposive sampling approach was employed to collect data for this study, primarily to secure a diverse sample encompassing various geographical regions and educational institutions. The universities included in this study are distributed across various regions, including Western, Eastern, and Central areas of the Chinese Mainland, ensuring geographical representation. Additionally, the universities included a range of prestige levels, encompassing tier 1 universities ('985' project) 4 , tier 2 universities ('211' project) 5 , and tier 3 universities (other institutions). This stratified selection deliberately captured a broad spectrum of the teaching and learning environment across different types of higher education institutions in China. 

Sample size was determined a-priori using the power analysis tool G*Power 3.1. A sample of 1,077 participants was found sufficient to detect a small effect size (0.1) with a 95% power and a 5% level of statistical significance (Faul et al. 2007). The online survey was distributed to university students through WeChat groups, a widely utilized communication platform in China. This distribution strategy was chosen to reach a varied student demographic, thereby maximizing the diversity of the data. Participants were instructed to carefully read the survey's purpose and the procedure for completing the questionnaire. Participation was entirely voluntary, allowing participants to withdraw at any time. We anonymized the survey without collecting identifiable information to reduce social desirability bias. 

Procedures in this study were approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of The University of Hong Kong (Approval number EA210512).

Title: Leveraging Interactive Evolutionary Computation to Induce Serendipity in Informal Learning
Snippet: While this study has met its objectives, it is not without limitations, which we acknowledge. Constructing recommender systems aimed at suggesting serendipitous items presents inherent challenges, as what constitutes serendipity for a user and how to generalize this across diverse learning activities remain open questions. 

In this study, to assess the effectiveness of the proposed system in promoting serendipitous learning experiences, we explicitly asked users to rate the interestingness of the presented paths on a scale of 0 to 5 during their interaction with the system. This approach allowed us to directly track users' perceptions of the quality and relevance of the recommended contents. However, the evaluation primarily focused on user interest and overall perceptions of serendipity, leaving room for a more granular assessment of the novelty and unexpectedness of individual recommended paths in future studies. While user interest is a crucial factor in assessing the system's performance, it does not fully capture the nuances of serendipity, such as the degree of surprise or the extent to which the recommended paths deviate from users' expectations. 

Moreover, serendipity was measured using only two post-task questions, providing only a high-level indicator of users' overall serendipitous experiences. We acknowledge that this approach, while informative, may not fully capture the complex and multifaceted nature of serendipity in learning contexts. 

To address these limitations, future research should conduct more extensive evaluations that separately probe the novelty, unexpectedness, and serendipity of specific paths. This could involve asking users to rate each recommended path along these distinct dimensions, enabling a more fine-grained analysis of the system's serendipity-inducing capabilities. Additionally, gathering qualitative user feedback through interviews or open-ended survey questions could provide deeper insights into how users perceive and experience the system's recommendations. 

By combining quantitative ratings with qualitative feedback, future studies can gain a more comprehensive understanding of how the system's recommendations are experienced and identify specific aspects that contribute to or hinder serendipitous learning experiences. This knowledge can then inform further enhancements to the system's algorithms and user interface, ultimately improving its ability to promote serendipity in informal learning contexts.
</snippet>

Title: Leveraging Interactive Evolutionary Computation to Induce Serendipity in Informal Learning
Snippet: The experience of serendipity can also enhance perceived competence, as learners feel capable of making valuable discoveries on their own [28]. 

Moreover, constructivist learning theories emphasize the role of active exploration, experimentation, and personal meaning-making in the learning process [29]. Serendipitous encounters with new information and ideas can stimulate learners to construct their own knowledge by integrating novel insights with their existing understanding. This process of knowledge construction is particularly relevant in informal learning settings, where learners have greater control over their learning goals and trajectories [30]. 

However, it is important to acknowledge that the benefits of serendipity in informal learning may vary depending on individual learner characteristics, such as prior knowledge, learning style, and openness to experience [31].

Below is a practical toolkit of validated questionnaires, scales, and design tools to assess and steward an "Intentional University"—an ecosystem that balances purposeful, goal-directed learning with intentional design for serendipity and discovery. The instruments are grouped by construct (intentionality, learning processes, serendipity/discovery, social/relational climate, and enabling environments), with guidance on use and caveats.

1) What "Intentional University" asks us to measure
- Intentionality and self-regulated learning: goal-directed learning behaviors, learning intentions, self-efficacy, and personal resolve.
- Serendipity and discovery: frequency and quality of unexpected, valuable insights; novelty/unexpectedness and usefulness of encounters.
- Social/relational climate: relating to others, community and mentoring affordances that catalyze discovery.
- Equity and belonging: perceived fairness in opportunities, processes, and outcomes as prerequisites for engaged intentionality.
- Enabling environments: physical and digital spaces that restore attention, support exploration, and enable chance encounters.

2) Psychometric instruments adapted for higher-education contexts

Intentionality, motivation, and self-regulation
- Personal resolve and self-efficacy (adapted Likert scales). Example items operationalize "I will do whatever it takes to master my academic studies" and "I expect to do well academically," with reliability estimates around .70–.85 in university samples; these capture students' intentions and self-efficacy for academic learning and can be used to benchmark goal-directed engagement on your campus. <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">We used existing Likert-scale inventories to measure concepts; Personal Resolve and Personal Self-Efficacy were adapted from established sources with reliability estimates .85 and .72 respectively, showing feasibility for higher-education measurement</cite>.
- Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) subscales (adapted). The MSLQ's self-efficacy and self-regulation subscales are frequently adapted for university surveys; they provide validated item pools to assess goal-setting, effort regulation, and volitional control central to intentional learning. <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">Personal Self-Efficacy was adapted from the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (Pintrich et al., 1993)</cite>.

Serendipity and serendipitous learning
- Operationalized serendipity items (novelty, unexpectedness, usefulness). Studies report using paired post-task Likerts and open-ended probes to capture perceived interestingness, novelty, and unexpectedness of recommendations or encounters; combining quantitative ratings with qualitative feedback helps parse the components of serendipity experienced in learning systems and spaces. <cite id="b3bef86f-0">Serendipity was measured with two post-task 0–5 ratings of interestingness; authors note this high-level indicator may miss novelty and unexpectedness, recommending item-level ratings and qualitative feedback to capture serendipity nuances</cite> <cite id="b3bef86f-1">Serendipity-enhancing systems can be designed by supporting internal, external factors, and exploratory behavior, providing a framework to operationalize serendipity in learning environments</cite>.
- Conceptual definitions to inform item development. Literature distinguishes serendipity as unexpected realizations of hidden connections, exploration guided by skills and goals, and by-product discoveries during planned tasks; these definitions support constructing items that target "unexpected yet valuable insights," "connecting unconnected ideas," and "productive tangents." <cite id="b3bef86f-2">Serendipitous learning emphasizes unexpected realization of hidden connections; surprising information and unexpected social relationships can lead to meaningful learning and enhance exploratory behavior</cite>.
- Minimal serendipity probes for pilots. Short Likert items plus one open question can quickly assess perceived usefulness of random exploration and serendipity in a campus or classroom context. <cite id="b3bef86f-3">Questionnaires can include 5-point Likert items on random exploration and serendipity plus an open question about usefulness, providing a lightweight operationalization</cite>.

Social/relational climate and belonging
- Relating to others (LOSO-based). Adapted LOSO items (e.g., "I find it easy to relate to others at university") provide a reliable measure of students' relational functioning and social connectedness; these can be used to assess mentoring, peer learning networks, and community climate that enable collaborative discovery. <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">Relating to Others was adapted from the LOSO Questionnaire (Van Damme et al., 2002) with reliability estimate .72</cite>.
- Social milieu and inclusion. Adapted items gauge whether the university milieu is welcoming and accepting of diversity—conditions that support intentional learning and openness to novel perspectives. <cite id="05fa2f3a-3">The Social Milieu subscale (adapted items) measured perceived welcoming and accepting climate with reliability estimate .83</cite>.
- Sense of educational equity. A validated 19-item questionnaire across three dimensions—equity in opportunities, process, and outcomes—offers a compact, well-tested instrument to assess whether students perceive fair access and treatment, which is foundational for intentional engagement and risk-taking in discovery. <cite id="f4706e52-1">A 19-item questionnaire on sense of equity (opportunities, process, outcomes) using a 5-point Likert scale showed Cronbach's alpha >.7 for each dimension</cite>.

Enabling environments: physical/digital spaces and restoration
- Rest@U: perceived restorativeness of the university environment. Title: First validation of the technical and administrative staff quality of life at work tool (TASQ@work) in academia
Snippet: Although the analyses conducted on the instrument confirm its good psychometric properties, there are some limitations that we aim to address and overcome with subsequent research. 

The first limitation concerns the invariance results with respect to the RMSEA index in some resources scales (work meaning, distributive justice, organizational support for work-life balance, organizational identification). Although the other indices are very good, the RMSEA exceeds the desired cut-off threshold. We believe that this limitation is related to the others mentioned so far and that with a larger sample size and more differentiation per university, we can improve the goodness of fit of this index. This is supported by a reflection on this index conducted by Kenny et al. (2015): the authors agree that when the degrees of freedom (df) and the sample (N) are small a "larger" RMSEA is easy (Kenny et al., 2015, p. 487). To assess the sampling error in the RMSEA, a confidence interval (CI) can be calculated (Kenny et al., 2015). Several groups of researchers have studied the performance of the RMSEA using simulations that      and Williams, 2011;Kenny et al., 2015). Therefore, by increasing the sample size in future surveys to be able to use the full range of variables in the theoretical model, we hope to overcome this important limitation. Now, we can identify an initial correct functioning of the scales within the university context as far as staff are concerned. 

The second limitation concerns the sample: the research we conducted is still at a preliminary stage and it is not possible to generalize the results. We could only examine the psychometric properties of the scales by comparing only two universities. Further analyses could extend the sample by considering other universities. Third, in this study we provide evidence of normality of the items, reliability, content, construct and nomological validity. Moreover we tested measurement invariance across gender, seniority, and Athenaeum. Although these are promising results, other kinds of validity should be tested in the future, such as convergent and criterion validity, and temporal reliability. Future research could also benefit from the use of this tool for testing longitudinally the J-DR model in the same Universities.

Title: Leveraging Interactive Evolutionary Computation to Induce Serendipity in Informal Learning
Snippet: While this study has met its objectives, it is not without limitations, which we acknowledge. Constructing recommender systems aimed at suggesting serendipitous items presents inherent challenges, as what constitutes serendipity for a user and how to generalize this across diverse learning activities remain open questions. 

In this study, to assess the effectiveness of the proposed system in promoting serendipitous learning experiences, we explicitly asked users to rate the interestingness of the presented paths on a scale of 0 to 5 during their interaction with the system. This approach allowed us to directly track users' perceptions of the quality and relevance of the recommended contents. However, the evaluation primarily focused on user interest and overall perceptions of serendipity, leaving room for a more granular assessment of the novelty and unexpectedness of individual recommended paths in future studies. While user interest is a crucial factor in assessing the system's performance, it does not fully capture the nuances of serendipity, such as the degree of surprise or the extent to which the recommended paths deviate from users' expectations. 

Moreover, serendipity was measured using only two post-task questions, providing only a high-level indicator of users' overall serendipitous experiences. We acknowledge that this approach, while informative, may not fully capture the complex and multifaceted nature of serendipity in learning contexts. 

To address these limitations, future research should conduct more extensive evaluations that separately probe the novelty, unexpectedness, and serendipity of specific paths. This could involve asking users to rate each recommended path along these distinct dimensions, enabling a more fine-grained analysis of the system's serendipity-inducing capabilities. Additionally, gathering qualitative user feedback through interviews or open-ended survey questions could provide deeper insights into how users perceive and experience the system's recommendations. 

By combining quantitative ratings with qualitative feedback, future studies can gain a more comprehensive understanding of how the system's recommendations are experienced and identify specific aspects that contribute to or hinder serendipitous learning experiences. This knowledge can then inform further enhancements to the system's algorithms and user interface, ultimately improving its ability to promote serendipity in informal learning contexts.

The first limitation concerns the invariance results with respect to the RMSEA index in some resources scales (work meaning, distributive justice, organizational support for work-life balance, organizational identification). Although the other indices are very good, the RMSEA exceeds the desired cut-off threshold. We believe that this limitation is related to the others mentioned so far and that with a larger sample size and more differentiation per university, we can improve the goodness of fit of this index. This is supported by a reflection on this index conducted by Kenny et al. (2015): the authors agree that when the degrees of freedom (df) and the sample (N) are small a "larger" RMSEA is easy (Kenny et al., 2015, p. 487). To assess the sampling error in the RMSEA, a confidence interval (CI) can be calculated (Kenny et al., 2015). Several groups of researchers have studied the performance of the RMSEA using simulations that      and Williams, 2011;Kenny et al., 2015). Now, we can identify an initial correct functioning of the scales within the university context as far as staff are concerned. 

The second limitation concerns the sample: the research we conducted is still at a preliminary stage and it is not possible to generalize the results. We could only examine the psychometric properties of the scales by comparing only two universities. Further analyses could extend the sample by considering other universities.
